267.title: Islam: one God
267.hook: the declaration of faith: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is God's messenger (Quran 112)
267.howItsDone: Muslims say the shahada in every daily prayer and hear it in every call to prayer; many whisper the call to prayer to a newborn and hope to say the shahada as their last words.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lent, and ashes on the forehead. Your line was forty days. Did you keep your one small fast? Day two hundred sixty-seven, and a new visit: Islam.

A baby is born in a hospital in Cairo, or Jakarta, or Birmingham, Alabama. Within minutes, in many Muslim families, a father or grandfather leans close to the newborn's ear and softly speaks the call to prayer. So among the first words that baby ever hears is a sentence about God. And at the other end of life, families gathered at a bedside hope the same sentence will be among the last words spoken. First breath to last, one sentence frames it all. Today, on our visit to Islam: the shahada.
screen: `A NEWBORN, A WHISPER IN THE EAR.` → `A BEDSIDE, THE LAST WORDS.` → `THE SHAHADA.`

segments.voice: Shahada means witness, or testimony. It's the declaration at the heart of Islam, naming God and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: la ilaha illa Allah, Muhammad rasul Allah. There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. Allah is simply the Arabic word for God; Arab Christians use it too. The shahada has two halves. The first is about God: that God is one, with no partner and no rival. Muslims call this oneness tawhid, and it's the center of everything else. The second is about the Prophet: that he is God's messenger, bringing the Qur'an. Saying the shahada sincerely, with understanding, is how a person becomes Muslim. It's the first of the five pillars of Islam, and it's repeated in every call to prayer, five times a day, from minarets around the world. The Qur'an puts God's oneness most memorably in one of its shortest chapters, surah one hundred twelve. In Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him." Four short lines. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet is reported to have said this little chapter equals a third of the Qur'an, and many Muslims recite it every day. Notice the shape: first a negation, no god, and then an affirmation, but God. Many Muslim teachers say the negation clears the ground, all the false centers a life can have, money, status, fear, and the affirmation leaves only one. One.
screen: `SHAHADA — WITNESS, TESTIMONY.` · `NO GOD BUT GOD: TAWHID.` · `MUHAMMAD, THE MESSENGER.` · `SAY: HE IS ALLAH, THE ONE.` · then, large: `ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with the word one. Breathe in, and let the mind be busy as it is. Breathe out, and quietly say, one. Each time a thought pulls at you, a worry, a plan, a craving, notice it, and come back: one. If you're Muslim, you might hold the shahada itself. If not, just let one be the only word in the room. The bell holds the time.
Shahada. Witness: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. The first pillar of Islam. Today's word.
Your line: one. Today, when your attention splits ten ways, pick one thing and give it all of you. Day two hundred sixty-seven.

268.title: Islam: five prayers
268.hook: Muslims pray five times a day, facing Mecca
268.howItsDone: Muslims pray salat five times a day at set times, after washing with wudu and facing the Kaaba in Mecca, alone or together; on Fridays the midday prayer is held in congregation at the mosque.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the shahada, there is no god but God. Your line was one. Did one thing get all of you? Day two hundred sixty-eight.

Your phone probably interrupts you a hundred times a day. Pings, buzzes, banners, each one pulling you toward something someone else wants. Now imagine a different kind of interruption, only five, spread from before dawn to after dark, and each one pulls you toward God. You stop what you're doing, wash, turn in one direction, and pray. And because the times follow the sun, as dawn and dusk move across the time zones, a wave of prayer rolls around the planet all day. Today, on our visit to Islam: salat, the five daily prayers.
screen: `A HUNDRED PINGS A DAY.` → `FIVE INTERRUPTIONS TOWARD GOD.` → `A WAVE AROUND THE PLANET.`

segments.voice: Salat is the second pillar of Islam, after the shahada. The five prayers have names, and they follow the sun. Fajr, before dawn. Dhuhr, just after midday. Asr, in the afternoon. Maghrib, just after sunset. Isha, at night. Before praying, Muslims wash in a set way, called wudu: hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, ears, feet. Then they face the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca. At first the early Muslims faced Jerusalem, and the Qur'an records the change of direction in its second chapter. Each prayer is made of cycles of standing, bowing, prostrating with the forehead on the ground, and sitting, reciting the Qur'an in Arabic, beginning with its opening chapter. Why five? A well-known hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tells of the night journey of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, when fifty daily prayers were first commanded. On the way back, Moses, the story goes, urged him to return and ask for fewer, and he went back again and again until they were five, with the reward of fifty. The Qur'an gives the purpose in a line to Moses himself. In Pickthall's 1930 translation, God says, "establish worship for My remembrance." So the five prayers are, among other things, a way to remember God five times, before the day can make you forget. Practice varies a little. Many Shia Muslims pray the five prayers in three sessions, joining some of them, and Sunni Muslims may join them when traveling. Mosques call people to each one, but the prayer can be made anywhere clean: an office, a park, an airport floor.
screen: `FAJR, DHUHR, ASR, MAGHRIB, ISHA.` · `WASH, THEN FACE THE KAABA.` · `FIFTY, BARGAINED DOWN TO FIVE.` · `ESTABLISH WORSHIP FOR MY REMEMBRANCE.` · then, large: `FIVE PAUSES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, a small version for now. Sit comfortably. Imagine your day with five pauses in it: waking, midday, afternoon, sunset, bedtime. For each one, picture yourself stopping for a single minute. If you pray, that minute can be prayer. If not, it can be a breath, a thank-you, turning your attention toward what matters most. Rehearse them now, one by one. The bell holds the time.
Salat. The five daily prayers, facing Mecca, from before dawn to after dark: the second pillar of Islam. Today's word.
Your line: five pauses. Today, set five small alarms if you like, and at each one stop for a minute and remember what matters. Day two hundred sixty-eight.

269.title: Islam: remembrance
269.hook: in the remembrance of God hearts find rest (Quran 13:28)
269.howItsDone: After each daily prayer many Muslims say subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar on their fingers or prayer beads, and Sufi communities gather for dhikr sessions of chanted remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salat, the five daily prayers. Your line was five pauses. How many did you manage? Day two hundred sixty-nine.

It's two in the morning and your mind won't stop. It replays the conversation from lunch, rehearses tomorrow's meeting, lists everything that could go wrong. You try to push the thoughts away and they come back louder. Anyone who has lain awake like that knows the heart can be the least restful place in the body. Now picture an old man in a mosque after the dawn prayer, beads slipping through his fingers, lips moving softly, the same few words again and again. He looks like the most rested person in the city. Today, on our visit to Islam: dhikr, remembrance.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, MIND RACING.` → `BEADS AFTER THE DAWN PRAYER.` → `DHIKR.`

segments.voice: Dhikr means remembrance, and also mention: to remember God, and to say God's name. The Qur'an asks for it often. One of its best-loved lines, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation, is today's: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" Hearts find rest. Not by solving everything, but by remembering. Another verse turns it into a two-way street: remember me, God says, and I will remember you. The simplest dhikr is short phrases. After each daily prayer, many Muslims say subhanallah, glory be to God, thirty-three times; alhamdulillah, praise be to God, thirty-three times; and Allahu akbar, God is greater, thirty-four times, counting on their fingers or on prayer beads called a misbaha or tasbih. A hadith tells that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught this to his daughter Fatima when she was exhausted from hard work and asked for a servant. He told her these words would be better for her than a servant. Dhikr can be silent or aloud, alone or together. Among Sufis, the mystical tradition within Islam, groups gather to chant God's names in rhythm, sometimes for hours, and some Sufi orders pair the words with the breath or with movement. Many Muslims keep a quiet dhikr going through the day: a phrase while waiting for the bus, while walking, while falling asleep. The idea is that the heart is always remembering something. Dhikr gives it something to remember that can hold its weight.
screen: `DHIKR — REMEMBRANCE, MENTION.` · `IN REMEMBRANCE, HEARTS FIND REST.` · `THIRTY-THREE, THIRTY-THREE, THIRTY-FOUR.` · `SILENT OR ALOUD, ALONE OR TOGETHER.` · then, large: `HEARTS FIND REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repeat one word slowly. Choose a word that settles you. If you're Muslim, it might be Allah, or alhamdulillah. If not, it can be peace, or here, or thank you. Breathe in. On the out-breath, say the word, silently or softly. Again. Again. When the mind runs off, don't scold it. Just return to the word. The bell holds the time.
Dhikr. Remembrance: short phrases said again and again, so that, as the Qur'an says, hearts find rest. Today's word.
Your line: hearts find rest. Tonight, if your mind starts racing, go back to your one word, and let it carry you toward sleep. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

270.title: Islam: begin with mercy
270.hook: almost every chapter opens: in the name of God, most gracious, most merciful (Quran 1:1)
270.howItsDone: Muslims recite the basmala at the start of each chapter of the Qur'an and say bismillah before eating, traveling, working and many ordinary acts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhikr, remembrance, one word said again and again. Your line was hearts find rest. Did your word carry you anywhere? Day two hundred seventy.

Think about how you start things. An email: per my last message. A hard conversation: we need to talk. A Monday: with a groan. The first words set the weather for everything after them. Now open a Qur'an. Turn to almost any chapter, one hundred thirteen of its one hundred fourteen, and before anything else, before law or story or warning, you'll find the same opening line. It names God, and then, twice over, it names mercy. Today, on our visit to Islam: Rahman, and the habit of beginning with mercy.
screen: `PER MY LAST MESSAGE.` → `THE SAME FIRST LINE, 113 TIMES.` → `MERCY, TWICE OVER.`

segments.voice: The line is called the basmala, and it opens the very first chapter. In Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." In Arabic: bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim. Two names for God, and both grow from the same three-letter root, r-h-m. Rahman is the vast, overflowing mercy that covers everything and everyone. Rahim is the steady, caring mercy that stays close. Scholars have written whole books on the difference. And here is what surprises people: in Arabic, the same root gives the word rahim, the womb. A hadith reports God saying: I am ar-Rahman; I created the womb and gave it a name drawn from my own. Mercy, in this language, is the love of a mother for the child she carries. Another hadith, in Sahih al-Bukhari, says that when God created the world, God wrote: my mercy prevails over my wrath. And another, that God divided mercy into a hundred parts and sent just one down to earth; from that single part, a mother animal lifts her hoof so as not to hurt her young. Only one chapter, the ninth, doesn't open with the basmala, and scholars give different reasons. But the line appears again inside chapter twenty-seven, in a letter from Solomon, so the count comes out at one hundred fourteen. Muslims say bismillah before eating, driving, starting work, even entering a room. Beginning with God's name is beginning with mercy, and many Muslims say it sets the weather for what follows.
screen: `THE BASMALA OPENS THE BOOK.` · `RAHMAN AND RAHIM: ONE ROOT.` · `RAHIM — THE WOMB.` · `MY MERCY PREVAILS OVER MY WRATH.` · then, large: `BEGIN WITH MERCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin one task with a kind word. Sit, and think of the next thing you'll start: a message, a meeting, a chore, a conversation with someone difficult. Picture its first words. Now soften them. Replace per my last message with thanks for this. Replace we need to talk with I've been thinking about you. If you pray, you might begin with bismillah. The bell holds the time.
Rahman. The Most Merciful: mercy that overflows, from the same root as the word for womb, named at the start of almost every chapter. Today's word.
Your line: begin with mercy. Today, open your next hard message or conversation with one kind sentence, and see how the weather changes. Day two hundred seventy.

271.title: Islam: giving
271.hook: a set share of wealth goes each year to those in need
271.howItsDone: Muslims whose savings exceed the nisab for a lunar year give zakat, usually two and a half percent, directly or through mosques and charities; many pay it in Ramadan and give zakat al-fitr before the Eid prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rahman, the Most Merciful, and the line that opens the chapters. Your line was begin with mercy. Did a kind first sentence change the weather? Day two hundred seventy-one.

Most of us think of giving as something extra. The coin in the cup when we happen to have one. The fundraiser link we tap when a friend shares it. Nice, occasional, optional. Now imagine giving that works more like rent. Every year, you sit down with a calculator, add up your savings, and a set share of it goes to people in need. Not whenever you feel moved. Every year, on a schedule, as part of your religion. For well over a billion people, this is simply how it's done. Today, on our visit to Islam: zakat.
screen: `A COIN IN THE CUP.` → `A CALCULATOR, ONCE A YEAR.` → `ZAKAT.`

segments.voice: Zakat is the third pillar of Islam, after the shahada and the prayer; in the Qur'an, the command to pray and the command to give zakat often come in the same breath. Here's how it works. If a Muslim's savings stay above a minimum amount, called the nisab, for a full lunar year, they give a portion, most commonly two and a half percent, to those in need. Scholars have long worked out the details for gold, crops, livestock and trade goods. The Qur'an names who can receive it, including the poor, the needy, people in debt, travelers stranded far from home, and those working to free captives. Now the word, because it's the key. Zakat comes from a root that means both to purify and to grow. The Qur'an says to the Prophet, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow." Purify them: not the money, the people. The giving cleans the giver's heart of greed and the fear of not having enough. And a hadith in Sahih Muslim says charity never decreases wealth. Alongside zakat, which is required, there is sadaqah, voluntary giving, which can be anything. A well-known hadith counts even a smile to your brother as sadaqah. So zakat is the floor, set and dependable; sadaqah has no ceiling. Many Muslims pay their zakat during Ramadan, when rewards are believed to be greater, and there is a special gift of food before the prayer at the end of Ramadan, so everyone can celebrate.
screen: `THE THIRD PILLAR, BESIDE PRAYER.` · `A SET SHARE, ONCE A YEAR.` · `ZAKAT — TO PURIFY, TO GROW.` · `ZAKAT THE FLOOR, SADAQAH NO CEILING.` · then, large: `PURIFIED BY GIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to give something today. Sit, and notice what you have more than enough of. Money, maybe, but also time, food in the cupboard, clothes you don't wear, attention. Notice any tightness when you think of giving it away. That tightness is what the word zakat is about. Choose one thing, and one person or cause to give it to. The bell holds the time.
Zakat. A set share of wealth given each year to those in need, from a root meaning to purify and to grow. The third pillar. Today's word.
Your line: purified by giving. Today, give the one thing you chose, and notice whether it leaves you lighter. Day two hundred seventy-one.

272.title: Islam: good character
272.hook: Muslims honor the Prophet's gentleness, and a hadith says the best of you are the best in character (Bukhari)
272.howItsDone: Muslims study akhlaq, Islamic ethics, alongside prayer and law, and many learn the Prophet's example of gentleness from the hadith collections and biographies taught in mosques and families.

segments.voice: Yesterday: zakat, the yearly share for those in need. Your line was purified by giving. Did giving leave you lighter? Day two hundred seventy-two.

Picture the mosque in Medina, the Prophet's own mosque, with his companions sitting around him. A desert traveler wanders in, a Bedouin who doesn't know the customs, walks to a corner, and starts to relieve himself on the floor. The companions leap up, shouting, ready to drag him out. And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stops them. Let him finish, he says. Then he has a bucket of water poured over the spot, and he calls the man over and explains, kindly, what a mosque is for. Today, on our visit to Islam: good character.
screen: `A STRANGER IN THE MOSQUE.` → `THE COMPANIONS LEAP UP.` → `LET HIM FINISH.`

segments.voice: That story is in Sahih al-Bukhari, and in one version the Prophet tells his companions: you were sent to make things easy, not to make them difficult. It's one of many. Muslims remember him for his gentleness: mending his own shoes, helping at home, playing with children, standing up when a funeral passed. The Qur'an says to him, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature." The Arabic word there is khuluq, character, from the same family as akhlaq, the Muslim word for ethics and good conduct. When his wife Aisha was later asked what his character was like, she answered, in a report in Sahih Muslim: his character was the Qur'an. In other words, he lived what he recited. And he put character at the very top. In a hadith in Bukhari, he says: the best of you are those who are best in character. Another hadith says nothing will be heavier on the scale on the Day of Judgment than good character. And another, reported in several collections, has him describe his whole mission as coming to perfect good character. So in Islam, character is not a pleasant extra added to prayer and fasting. It's what prayer and fasting are for. A hadith warns that someone who fasts but doesn't give up lying and cruelty has missed the point of fasting. That's a thread we'll pick up tomorrow. The Bedouin in the mosque learned more from the bucket of water than from any shout.
screen: `MAKE THINGS EASY, NOT DIFFICULT.` · `THOU ART OF A TREMENDOUS NATURE.` · `HIS CHARACTER WAS THE QUR'AN.` · `NOTHING HEAVIER ON THE SCALE.` · then, large: `BEST IN CHARACTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle once today, starting in your imagination. Sit, and recall a moment when someone did something wrong in front of you and you wanted to shout. Replay it. This time, picture the pause. Let him finish. Then picture the bucket of water: the practical fix, and a kind explanation. Breathe, and let the gentler version settle in. The bell holds the time.
Islam, through good character: akhlaq, the gentleness Muslims honor in the Prophet. The best of you are the best in character. Today's word.
Your line: best in character. Today, when someone gets it wrong, try the Medina way: pause, fix it simply, explain it kindly. Day two hundred seventy-two.

273.title: Ramadan, the fasting month
273.hook: a month of fasting from dawn to sunset, with prayer and generosity (Quran 2:183)
273.howItsDone: During Ramadan adult Muslims who are able fast from dawn to sunset, eat suhur before dawn and break the fast at iftar, often with dates and water, add night prayers, give generously, and celebrate Eid al-Fitr at the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday: good character, and the bucket of water in Medina. Your line was best in character. Did you pause before the shout? Day two hundred seventy-three, the last day of our visit to Islam.

It's a few minutes before sunset in a city apartment. The table is set, but no one's eating. A plate of dates, a jug of water, soup on the stove. The whole family is watching the clock, or listening for the call to prayer from the mosque down the street. Nobody has eaten or drunk anything since before dawn, not even a sip of water, and it's been a long, hot day. Then the call comes, someone passes the dates, and a whole city breaks its fast in the same minute. Today, to end our week with Islam: Ramadan.
screen: `DATES, WATER, WATCHING THE CLOCK.` → `NOTHING SINCE BEFORE DAWN.` → `A CITY BREAKS ITS FAST.`

segments.voice: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, which follows the moon, so it moves about eleven days earlier each year, through every season. Fasting in it is the fourth pillar of Islam. The Qur'an gives the command, in Marmaduke Pickthall's 1930 translation: "O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)." Even as for those before you: the Qur'an sets the fast alongside the fasting of earlier believers. From dawn to sunset, adult Muslims who are able go without food, drink and marital relations. There are exemptions: the sick, travelers, the elderly, those pregnant or nursing, children. A pre-dawn meal, suhur, starts the day; the iftar, often begun with dates and water as the Prophet did, ends it. Why this month? The Qur'an says Ramadan is the month in which the Qur'an was sent down, and many Muslims try to recite all of it during the month, with extra night prayers in the mosque. Somewhere in the last ten nights falls the Night of Power, which the Qur'an calls better than a thousand months. And yesterday's thread returns: a hadith in Bukhari says that if someone fasts but doesn't give up false speech and acting on it, God has no need of their giving up food and drink. The hunger is meant to teach: patience, gratitude, what the poor feel every day. The month ends with Eid al-Fitr, a feast. Look back at our week. Shahada: one. Salat: five pauses. Dhikr: hearts find rest. Rahman: begin with mercy. Zakat: purified by giving. Good character. And Ramadan: hunger teaches.
screen: `THE NINTH MONTH, FOLLOWING THE MOON.` · `FASTING IS PRESCRIBED FOR YOU.` · `THE MONTH THE QUR'AN CAME DOWN.` · `GIVE UP FALSE SPEECH, TOO.` · then, large: `HUNGER TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, a small taste of it: skip one snack today and notice. Right now, sit and notice your body. Any hunger, any thirst, any restlessness. Don't fix it. Just watch it. Then think of someone for whom this feeling isn't chosen and doesn't end at sunset. Let the hunger teach you something about them. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Ramadan. The ninth month, of fasting from dawn to sunset, with prayer, the Qur'an and generosity: the fourth pillar. Today's word.
Your line: hunger teaches. Today, skip one snack, and when the craving comes, let it remind you of someone who is hungry. Day two hundred seventy-three. Tomorrow we visit Sikhism.
